\binom{2000}{1000} = \frac{2000!}{1000! \cdot 1000!}
\]

\[
E_p(n!) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k} \right\rfloor
\]

\[
E_p\left(\binom{2000}{1000}\right) = E_p(2000!) - 2E_p(1000!)
\]
Substituting Legendre's Formula:
\[
E_p\left(\binom{2000}{1000}\right) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{2000}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2\left\lfloor \frac{1000}{p^k} \right\rfloor \right)
\]
A prime \(p\) divides \(\binom{2000}{1000}\) if and only if this exponent is at least 1. The term inside the summation, \(\left\lfloor \frac{2000}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2\left\lfloor \frac{1000}{p^k} \right\rfloor\), is either 0 or 1. It equals 1 if the fractional part of \(\frac{1000}{p^k}\) is non-zero (i.e., \(p^k\) does not divide 1000), and 0 if \(p^k\) divides 1000. More precisely, using the property \(\lfloor 2x \rfloor - 2\lfloor x \rfloor \in \{0, 1\}\), the sum counts the number of carries when adding 1000 and 1000 in base \(p\). By Kummer's Theorem, the exponent is the number of carries when adding \(1000 + 1000\) in base \(p\).

We are looking for the largest three-digit prime \(p\) (i.e., \(p \le 997\)) such that \(E_p\left(\binom{2000}{1000}\right) \ge 1\). This means there must be at least one carry when adding \(1000 + 1000\) in base \(p\).
